claims.text: Thermomechanical and subsequent thermal treatments can tune grain size, dislocation density, and solute clustering in single-phase FCC Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni-family alloys.
Grain size, dislocation density, and solute clustering govern the strength-ductility balance in these alloys.
Lower-temperature or milder annealing preserves a finer, defect-rich microstructure.
A finer, defect-rich microstructure impedes dislocation motion and increases strength relative to the standard equiatomic quinary baseline.
Higher-temperature thermal treatments cause grain growth and reduce defect density.
Grain growth and reduced defect density caused by higher-temperature treatment lead to lower strength.
Annealing changes the microstructure through grain growth and the annihilation or rearrangement of dislocations.
Shorter-duration annealing retains higher dislocation densities and finer grains than longer-duration annealing.
Retained dislocations and fine grains act as barriers to dislocation motion and thereby increase yield strength.
Longer-duration annealing reduces barriers to dislocation motion and lowers strength.
Milder thermal treatments should increase yield strength relative to the equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni baseline processed under standard conditions.
Milder thermal treatments may improve strain hardening relative to the standard baseline.
More aggressive thermal treatments should produce significant grain coarsening, fewer dislocation obstacles, and reduced strength.
The proposed trends apply only within a processing window that retains a single FCC phase and avoids secondary-phase precipitation.

The quantitative relationship between annealing-induced microstructural evolution and mechanical properties may differ among quaternary and ternary alloy subsets because of solute-specific interactions.
